parts.text: The ticket's premise that this is computable from data tetel already holds survives contact with the code for every input this design needs, and the shape of that data decides most of the design.
Prose and claim logs both ship inside the snapshot beside the memo, every event in them is timestamped, and the citation edge a paragraph carries is a field on the prose event itself.
Two details the ticket does not mention narrow what can be built.

Neither `prose::load_all` nor `claims::load_all` surfaces a timestamp — both replay their log into a struct that keeps only a revision count — so this check reads the JSONL directly rather than reusing the loaded types the rest of `check` works from.
And a prose block's id exists only inside the workspace:
`compose::render` writes the block's text and its `*cites:` marker and nothing else, so a residue line that says `P4` names something a reader holding only the memo cannot find.
Claim ids do not have that problem — the rendered ledger prints the workspace id verbatim.
NONE

llm_findings.clause: The ticket's premise that this is computable from data tetel already holds survives contact with the code for every input this design needs

parts.text: The ticket's phrase "the last grounding pass" is not merely ambiguous, as its own open questions suspected — read literally it is self-defeating, and this is the design's first and largest departure.

Every grounding pass is briefed on every claim in the ledger, whether or not it has been graded before, so a pass that finds nothing to change still appends a fresh record against the unchanged wording.

The two memos already in this tree show what that produces: one claim carrying ten records on a single unchanged digest, written by three passes across nearly half an hour, and another graded `qualifies` twice by different passes a quarter of an hour apart on text nobody touched.

Anchor the comparison at the most recent grading and the anchor walks forward every round; fix-round prose written in round three stops being "since the last pass" the moment round four runs, even though no pass has ever read a word of the prose.
On the ticket's own account of it, the trail this residue is named after ran six rounds.
So the anchor is the earliest record grading a claim's current wording — the moment that wording first entered proof.
A later pass over unchanged text cannot move it, and only a revision of the claim itself, followed by a grading of the new wording, ever does.
NONE
With the anchor fixed, the rule almost states itself, and the places where it does not are the places attack put there.

A prose block is listed when it is a paragraph rather than a heading, it cites at least one id, at least one cited id resolves to a ledger claim that is in proof, and the block's text timestamp is later than the latest first proof among those in-proof citations.
"In proof" is not a new predicate: it is the digest comparison `analyze_ledger` already performs, empty-digest grandfathering included.
The block's text timestamp is the earliest event in its history whose text and citation list both equal the current ones.
Neither half of that definition was in the first draft of this design and neither is decoration — the next two sections are about what each one closes.
The two quantifier choices the ticket left open fall out of the anchor rather than being decided by taste.
Per claim, take the earliest in-proof record, because that is when the wording settled.

Per block, take the latest of those, because a block is not anchored until its evidence base has settled — taking the earliest instead would list every paragraph whose text merely postdates its first-graded citation, which is nearly all of them.
Both memos already in this tree list nothing, and that includes the two real post-pass prose revisions they contain between them, tet29's P4 and tet28's P18.

Each was rewritten in a fix round after a pass had run, and each is correctly silent for the same reason: each also cites a claim revised in that same round, whose new wording entered proof only afterwards.
The maximum is doing exactly the work it was chosen for.

That also means the listing behaviour had to be tested on constructions appended to those logs rather than on a real defect: move a tet29 paragraph past its claim's first proof and touch no claim, and it is listed alone.
NONE

On the ticket's first open question — creation or revision — the residue is about neither act specifically but about the text's age: the timestamp is derived from the block's events without caring whether the earliest one bearing its current wording was a creation or a rewrite.

The exposure is the same in both directions, since a paragraph written fresh under already-graded claims rests on them exactly as ungradedly as a rewritten one, and the ticket's own vector could have arrived either way.

Counting creations also cannot inflate the list through paragraphs added to carry a new assertion under a new claim, and the reason is mechanical rather than statistical: a claim not yet in proof cannot anchor a block at all, and once a pass has put it in proof that first proof necessarily postdates a paragraph written before the pass ran.
How often a fix-round paragraph takes that shape rather than resting on old claims is a question about how authors behave, and nothing here measures it.
What creation-counting does catch is the case worth catching: a new paragraph written under nothing but old, settled claims.
NONE

llm_findings.clause: nothing here measures it

parts.text: What clears a listing is the whole design, and it took two refutations to get right.

Start with what is easy: a further grounding pass over unchanged wording appends records but cannot move the earliest one, so no amount of re-grounding clears a block — which is correct, since a grounding pass never reads the prose and could not vouch for it if it did.
The first refutation was that reverting a paragraph could not clear it either.
Prose history is append-only, so a revert appends a later timestamp; keyed on the last event, restoring the settled wording would have left the listing standing forever.
Looking the timestamp up by content rather than by event order fixes that.
The second refutation is sharper and came from attacking the fix.

Keyed on text alone, an author could leave the text untouched and revise only the citations — an act `prose::revise` does not even inspect, and one the `cite` parameter was added to permit — pointing the paragraph at some claim the fix round had legitimately revised and regraded.
The anchor moved forward, the timestamp stayed frozen, the line went out, and the machine partition stayed green.
A residue that can be silenced by an act indistinguishable from good authoring is worse than no residue, because it certifies.
Keying the timestamp on the text and the citation list together closes it: change either and the timestamp moves with it.

A third construction closed with it — an old uncited paragraph handed a citation to an already-settled claim, which under the earlier rule entered the list with a timestamp predating everything and was permanently unlistable.
So two things clear a listing: restoring the text and citations the claims settled under, and revising or adding a cited claim and having the new wording graded.
The second is precisely what the finding asks for, because the defect being surfaced is prose asserting something no claim carries.
The cost is that neither is cheap, and it is worth being blunt about how large it can get.

Nothing in the rule bounds the number of blocks it can reach: an author who flow-edits every paragraph of a settled memo will see every paragraph listed, and on a memo shaped like tet29 — twelve blocks, every one a cited paragraph, no headings among them — that is all twelve.
So what separates this from the `no scope declared` line that once printed once per claim is not that a full sweep is impossible.
It is that a full sweep here would report something the author did, not something tetel is; that it is about this document rather than about the tool; and that two concrete acts clear it.
NONE
Of everything the ticket left open, the doubt about comparing timestamps across workspaces is the one that deserved its suspicion, and it does not dissolve.
The claim to be careful with is what exactly is new here.
Ordering timestamps written by different processes is not: the mint-window check already places refusals against a mint, and each of those lines was appended by a separate invocation.

What is new is that the two sides come from different *workspaces* — one authoring, one grounding — where every existing comparison has stayed inside one, and where every check that could have compared a claim against its evidence used a digest instead.

The comparison is sound in unit: both timestamps come from a `now_unix` whose body is token-for-token the same in the only two places the worktree defines it, so the same epoch and the same unit with no timezone term between them.
What nothing in either record establishes is that the two processes read the same wall clock.

The bound that follows is exact, and the design's position is that it must be printed rather than left implicit: a reported ordering can be wrong only if the grounding process's clock differed from the authoring workspace's by more than the interval between the prose edit and the pass that first put the cited claims in proof.

Choosing first proof over last pass is what makes that interval a grounding round rather than seconds in the case this residue exists for — but nothing measured here bounds it from below, and no claim is made that it is always large.
NONE

llm_findings.clause: where every existing comparison has stayed inside one
where every check that could have compared a claim against its evidence used a digest instead

parts.text: So the question becomes whether the digest-shaped alternative the ticket hoped for exists.
Two were examined; both fail, and no claim is made that a third could not be found.
The sharp one — a record carrying a digest of the prose it vouches for, the exact analogue of `out_of_proof` — cannot be built, for a structural reason rather than an oversight.
`out_of_proof` compares digests because a record carries a digest of the very text it graded.
No record names or digests a prose block anywhere in its shape, and the brief a pass receives is id, proposition and pin.
Putting a prose digest into a record would mean the grounding pass reading the prose it exists to grade blind, which trades the independence the whole loop is built on for a residue line.
The weaker one is genuinely constructible and was worked through rather than waved away:

`render --out` could append a publication record — each prose block's text digest, each claim's proposition digest and whether anything grades it — and the residue would then be an ordinal comparison between successive publications with no clock in it at all.
It is rejected on resolution, and the reason is structural too.
A log that samples only when the author renders cannot order two events that fall inside one interval, and a grading followed by a prose edit followed by a single render is one interval.
On the ticket's own account, that is the shape the finding took.
The clock-free formulation would have been silent on it.
That is the trade, stated plainly: the timestamp comparison buys the one ordering an interval-sampled log cannot, and pays for it with a bound it prints.
NONE
The vacuous case needs no special handling, because the in-proof test already does the work — but which test turned out to matter, and attack decided it rather than argument.
A memo with no evidence ledger, and a memo halfway through its first draft, list nothing: no cited claim is in proof, so there is no first proof to compare against.

The design first required *every* cited claim to be in proof, on the tidy-looking ground that a paragraph resting on an ungrounded claim is already in front of the reader under a line about that claim.
It is not the same reader service — `ungrounded:

C99` is a line about a claim, not about the paragraph — and worse, it made adding a record-less citation a way to silence any listing at all, with a clean machine partition, since a claim with no records is human-owed rather than out of proof.
So the test is existential: one in-proof citation is enough to anchor a block, and a record-less citation contributes nothing to the anchor and cannot suppress anything.
Non-overlap survives for what is still skipped — a block every one of whose citations is ungrounded or out of proof is already reported, under `ungrounded` or under a machine failure.
Two populations remain outside the rule entirely.
Headings, which cite nothing by construction, and paragraphs that cite nothing by choice.

The second is a real gap: an uncited paragraph is the one place a false assertion can sit with no citation edge to compare it against, and that belongs in the printed non-coverage list rather than in a footnote here.
NONE

The last open question asks whether this is a line or a section, and the answer is neither exactly: it is bullets in the flat human-owed list, one per listed block, with a single preamble bullet ahead of them.
There are no sub-headings in that partition today, so a section would be the only one and would announce by its shape that it outranks everything beside it.

The preamble carries the one thing constant across the entries — that the ordering rests on two clocks nothing here can prove are the same — and it is printed once rather than per bullet for the reason this crate already recorded when it collapsed `no scope declared` to a single document-level line: repeating a constant per row buries the findings that are actually about the document.

Each entry names the block's workspace id and the line in this document where its text begins, because a block's id is never written into the rendered output and an id alone points at something the reader cannot find; that mapping comes from one new function in `compose`, consumed by `render`, so the block-to-line correspondence is described once.

The entry then names each cited claim with its first-proof timestamp and the pass that wrote it, and the block's own timestamp — the inputs to the comparison, printed so a reader can disagree with the conclusion rather than having to trust it.
NONE

Everything the implementer touches is declared in the modification-target section above, and there are six symbols: a field on `Findings`; a new `prose_after_proof`; the call to it inside `check_file`'s existing snapshot block, whose other occupants are the note-versus-extent check, the tree-state findings, the census and premise re-verifications and the mint windows; a `block_offsets` in `compose` that `render` consumes; the print loop and one added clause in the human-owed scope sentence; and the new `NON_COVERAGE` entries.
That block is where this finding's neighbours live; it is not everything in `check` that touches a snapshot, since the drift check and the authoring-identity read reach into one from outside it.
One instruction in the list is worth stating precisely, because getting it wrong fails silently.
The check has two inputs: the snapshot's `prose.jsonl`, read directly because the loader discards timestamps, and the claims and evidence `check_file` already holds.

Those claims must be the ones `check_file` imports from the rendered document, never the snapshot's `claims.jsonl` — every digest on record was computed over a ledger-derived proposition, and the two are not the same string, since rendering replaces newlines with spaces and importing trims every cell.
Implemented against the workspace log, the check would find no matching digest for such a claim, conclude it is not in proof, and drop every block citing it, with nothing red to say so.
`machine_check_failed` is untouched, which is what makes the line human-owed by construction rather than by good intentions.
Nothing new ships in the snapshot; no schema changes; nothing is executed and no file the document names is opened, so `check`'s standing guarantees hold unchanged.
Without a snapshot the list is simply not computed, in silence, exactly as the note-versus-extent check and the mint windows are not.
Five things go into the printed non-coverage list.
False prose that ships alongside a claim revision, which the ticket concedes and this design does not fix.
A paragraph that cites nothing.
A citation added to a claim not yet in proof, which cannot be listed, because by the time any pass proves that claim its first proof postdates the edit.
Whether the two clocks agree.
And whether the prose is wrong, which nothing here judges and nothing here should.
NONE
One property is worth settling explicitly, because it is where a rule of this family usually goes wrong: the trigger interprets no English.
It is not keyed on deciding from a memo's prose that the memo is in scope.
The citation edge is a field the author set with `--cites`, the heading flag is a boolean on the same event, and the ordering is a comparison of integers taken off two logs.
Text is consumed in exactly two places, and both are byte comparisons.

The in-proof test feeds a claim's proposition into sha256; and finding a block's text timestamp means testing each of its past versions for equality with the current text and citation list, which reads every version of every paragraph as bytes.
Nothing anywhere parses a sentence, matches a phrase, or forms a view about what a paragraph is about.
What stays undecidable is the verdict rather than the trigger: whether a listed paragraph really does assert something its claims do not carry.
That is not narrowed, hinted at or scored here.
It goes whole to the reader, which is what the human-owed partition is — the one whose own opening sentence ends "none of this is settled by a passing check".
NONE
One measurement made in passing deserves recording, because the next ticket in this family will meet it.
Declaring these six targets required six whole-worktree searches, and a census captures its entire output into a fact that ships in the snapshot.

This repository's previous two snapshots hold whole file dumps on single JSON lines — tet29's longest is 57249 bytes, tet28's 34477 — so a search for a symbol this crate discusses re-captures those dumps.
What such a search costs turns out to be a property of the instrument and the moment rather than of the symbol, in two separate ways.
`render` matches 486 lines and 373271 bytes of this tree in the state the census was taken in, or 447 and 311672 with `.git/` and `target/` excluded as well;
`NON_COVERAGE` 35 and 95637, `Findings` 23 and 57418, `check_file` 5 and 285, and the two symbols that do not exist yet nothing at all.
Those numbers hold still because the trees they range over are frozen.
Time: the same counts taken with this memo's own artifacts included do not hold still at all.

`render` measured 529 lines and 1136689 bytes at one point in this memo's review and 550 and 1202134 later, with no source change in between — what grew was this memo's evidence log, now 59 records and 164392 bytes, and its snapshot, whose longest fact line is the 574898-byte capture of the `render` census itself.
Grading a claim about census cost enlarges the thing the claim is about, which is the compounding thesis demonstrating itself.

It is also the one part of this section no independent pass can confirm, along with the count of six searches: both range over this memo's own logs and snapshot, which a pass grading this memo must not open, so they are recorded here expecting to stay ungraded.

What any pass can check, and what survives every way of scoping the count, is the ordering and its cause: censusing a symbol quoted at length in prior memos' captured snapshots costs orders of magnitude more than censusing one that appears only in source.

`check_file` is this crate's own entry point, dispatched from both front ends, and returns 5 lines and 285 bytes — so what drives the cost is not whether the crate talks about a symbol but whether earlier memos captured text quoting it, and every memo added under `docs/design/` enlarges the next memo's census of anything those memos quote.
NONE

parts.text: Every observation in this memo was taken against the tetel repository at commit e19a4694bedd1bd2bda91626362f9c2d05f35274, whose subject line is "transplant: select the donor's premises, and answer each one"; every claim below describes that tree, with one exception this memo states rather than hides — C13's time-varying figures were measured with this memo's own artifacts on disk, and no tet30 file exists at that commit.
TET-30 asks for one human-owed residue line in `check`: the prose blocks revised since the last grounding pass whose cited claims were not.
Not a refusal, no judgement about whether the prose is wrong, and computed rather than authored.
This memo settles what the anchor is, which timestamps are compared and across what, what the rule does with a memo nothing has graded, what the reader sees, and what the whole thing cannot see.

parts.text: The answer, up front.

Every input this design needs is present in data tetel already ships, so the mechanism is buildable — but the ticket's anchor is wrong in a way that would have made it silent on the very finding it cites.

"Since the last grounding pass" walks forward every round, because every pass is briefed on every claim and re-grades unchanged wording, so fix-round prose stops being recent as soon as another round runs.

The anchor is therefore the earliest record grading a claim's current wording — the moment that wording first entered proof — and a block is listed when its text postdates the latest such moment among the claims it cites that are in proof.

That single change settles the ticket's other ambiguities as side effects: it decides earliest-versus-latest in both quantifiers, it empties the vacuous cases without a special rule, it makes creation and revision the same question, and it stops a grounding pass from blessing prose it never read.
Two smaller corrections were forced by attack rather than reached by design, and both are on the other side of the comparison.

A block's timestamp is looked up by its text *and* its citation list together, not by its last event: keyed on the event, restoring a paragraph's settled wording could never clear the line, and keyed on text alone, a citation-only revision could silence one in seconds using a claim the fix round had legitimately produced.
And the in-proof test is existential, because requiring every citation to be in proof let a single record-less citation suppress a block with nothing red to show for it.

What none of this removes is a cross-process clock comparison, which neither digest-shaped alternative examined here can replace, because no evidence record has anywhere to put a digest of prose and the pass that would compute one is required not to read it.
That bound is printed once, in a preamble above the entries it qualifies.
NONE

This memo was written against a single tree: commit b57bf8edb4c1eb59d8d86a8327179f43a9cb0829, "design: anchor the residue at first proof, not at the last pass", with no tracked source file differing from it.
The reader who wants to re-take an observation should check that pin out first.
Which tree each individual observation was actually taken against is not something this memo asserts — every observation carries its own working-tree marker, and `check` prints those states.
NONE
The ticket asserts that the implementation is small because `look_grep` already shells out to `grep -r -I -n -H` and both greps CI runs support `--exclude-dir` and `--exclude`.
Half of that is right and can be shown here.

The binary `Command::new("grep")` resolves to on this machine is /usr/bin/grep, BSD grep 2.6.0-FreeBSD, with no GNU grep shadowing it under that name; it accepts both flags alongside the flag set `look_grep` already passes;
`--exclude-dir='*.tetel'` prunes snapshot directories at any depth and `--exclude='*.evidence.jsonl'` drops evidence ledgers.
The other half cannot be shown here at all.
Nothing in this memo was executed against GNU grep or on Linux, so the ticket's clause about the Linux grep is not verified by this design, and no claim in it asserts anything about that grep.
That is a bound, stated, not an omission.
NONE

llm_findings.clause: `--exclude-dir='*.tetel'` prunes snapshot directories at any depth

parts.text: The clause that is wrong is the one the ticket did not think it was making.
The ticket's first constraint — an explicitly named path must still be read, only traversal skips, "the rule `git` and `rg` apply to ignored files" — is stated as though grep already obeyed it.

A file named explicitly on grep's command line is skipped when `--exclude` matches it, and a directory named explicitly as the recursion root is skipped when `--exclude-dir` matches it; in both cases the identical command without the flag finds the match, so the flag is what removed it.
Exactly one of the three arrangements behaves the way the constraint describes, and it is the one nobody would have doubted:
`--exclude-dir` does not suppress a file that is named explicitly and searched non-recursively from inside an excluded directory.
So the explicit-path exception is not something this design can obtain by choosing flags.
It has to be implemented in tetel, above grep, by deciding when to pass the flags at all.
NONE
The rendered-memo test has a second problem, and it is in the ticket's one-line implementation sketch rather than in its principle.
The sketch says: glob for `*.tetel` directories under the search root, strip the suffix, pass the result as `--exclude`.
Both halves of that fail.

A `--exclude` pattern is matched against the name grep constructs for the file from the root it was given, so with a relative root an absolute-path pattern excludes nothing whatsoever and the search silently returns everything, while the same file spelled relative to the root is excluded correctly.

And a suffix-stripped bare basename is not a name — it is a glob that matches that basename anywhere in the tree, which in the measurement removed both a real rendered memo and an unrelated file of the same name that has no snapshot beside it and so is not a memo at all.
A wrong exclusion of that second kind is the worst failure available here, because it hides source from a census under the banner of hiding tetel's own output.
The pattern must be emitted path-prefixed, in whatever spelling the root itself was given in.
NONE

llm_findings.clause: with a relative root an absolute-path pattern excludes nothing whatsoever
the search silently returns everything
it is a glob that matches that basename anywhere in the tree

parts.text: The disclosure goes in the whole-search record's label, and it costs nothing in schema.

TET-28 already added exactly one record per `look --grep` whose job is to say where a search started rather than what it hit — a `Search` entry when the grep matched, a `NoMatch` entry when it did not, and never both.
That record is the natural and the only correct home for a statement about what the search did not visit, because the exclusion is a property of the search and not of any file it found.

Putting the text there buys two carriers already built: the memo's Facts table renders each extent entry's label and renders nothing else from it, so the exclusion set is on the page for a reader who has only the committed document; and the pin hashes the label, so two searches with different exclusion sets fingerprint differently even when the text they matched is identical.

It should also be printed in what `look` returns, for the author reading it in the moment — but the printed string is the convenience and the label is the record, which is the opposite of the two shapes this project has already been burned by: a warning with no lifecycle, and a refusal trail missing the refusal that mattered.
NONE
The ticket's numbers are figures reported inside a memo, which makes them claims that were graded rather than measurements anyone here has made, so the effect was re-measured on this tree directly.
A census of the symbol `NON_COVERAGE` over the tetel worktree returns 858,096 bytes from fifteen files.
Fourteen of those files are tetel's own output — three rendered memos, three evidence ledgers, eight snapshot logs — and one, `src/report.rs`, is the source anybody grepping for that symbol wanted.
With the three exclusions the same census returns 169 bytes from `src/report.rs` alone.

Those are bytes grep handed back and bytes a fact would then store; what fraction of them reaches any given caller is a separate quantity, and a later section settles it, because the ticket's answer to it does not survive.
NONE
Against that, the enumeration the rendered-memo test requires is cheap in the only comparison that matters, which is against the grep it precedes.
It is a walk over directories; the grep is a walk over directories that opens and reads every file beneath them.
On this worktree — 848 directories against 159,519 files — the enumeration takes 0.130s and one census grep takes 3.953s.
So the answer to what happens on an enormous root is that the enumeration is dominated by the search it serves.
The answer for an unreadable root is that both stop at the same wall: a directory nobody can open produces the same permission error from each.
That is one failure mode, though, and it is the only one measured.

Whether the two walks agree on symlinked directories was not tested, and an implementer should not assume it — a difference there would mean the walk misses a snapshot the grep then reads, which is the one way this mechanism fails quietly rather than loudly.
NONE
This design ran into its own subject before it could declare a single modification target, and the shape of that is worth stating rather than working around quietly.
TET-28 requires a symbol an implementer is told to modify to be censused by a grep of the whole worktree.
Every candidate symbol here was priced first:
`look_grep` costs 709,469 bytes, `NON_COVERAGE` 858,096, `censuses` 691,562, `look_path` 688,776, `search_key` 633,291.
The interesting number is not any one of them but the floor they share — roughly 0.63 MB is returned whichever symbol is asked for, because it is not about the symbol at all.
Dropping snapshot directories and evidence ledgers alone removes between 95.9% and 99.9% of each.

So the census requirement is today priced by tetel's own accumulated output rather than by the code being censused: two thirds of a megabyte comes back from grep, and is stored in the fact, per declared target.
NONE
Then the design paid the price once, deliberately, to declare `look_grep` — and the payment failed in a way that settles the ticket's sharpest question.
The search ran and was recorded, but the harness returning results to the author refused to hand back 707,751 characters across 38 lines, and spilled them to a file.
So this memo's author never read the output of their own census, while the fact minted anyway and the full 707,751 characters are shipping in the snapshot beside this document.

The ticket asked any design to say which path it is changing, the return path or the retention path, and this is the answer from the inside: they are already separable, only the return path currently has a cap, that cap belongs to the harness rather than to tetel, and it fired.
The census's own extent is the summary of the problem — ten files matched, eight of them tetel's own output, two of them the source anyone grepping for `look_grep` was looking for.
NONE
The ticket's reframing — the one that moved it to the front of the queue — is that the primary cost is context, quantified as roughly 135k tokens and about 40% of a 336k run.
This design does not carry that figure, and the reason is not scepticism but a counter-instance produced in the course of the work.
`look_grep`'s return is uncapped in tetel exactly as the ticket says: the grep's whole stdout is copied into what the function hands back, with no length check or truncation anywhere between them.
But when this design took a real whole-worktree census, the client refused the 707,751-character result and returned about 1,300 characters of error text naming a spill file.
The bytes a census returns and the bytes that enter a model's context are therefore two quantities, and the second does not follow from the first.
Anyone wishing to restore the ticket's figure would have to measure the second directly, against a specific client, and say which.
NONE
What survives is a smaller argument and a better one, and it is the argument this design is built on.
The bound that fired was the caller's, not tetel's. tetel returns unbounded output and depends on whoever is holding it to decide that was too much; a different client will not decide anything.
That is a defect on its own terms, independent of any token arithmetic — and it is sharpened, not weakened, by how the truncation behaved here.

The client disclosed the skip to the author in the moment and left no trace of it anywhere in the fact, so the minted record now carries 707,751 characters of captured output that nobody read, with nothing in the extent saying so.
The ticket's own second constraint is that a skip must never be silent.
The one skip observed during this design was silent in exactly the way the constraint forbids, and it was not tetel's.
NONE
The change lands in one function, `look_grep`, and it is a decision about whether to pass exclusion flags at all rather than a decision about which flags to pass.
`look_grep` already distinguishes the two cases the rule needs: it adds `-r` only when the root is a directory, and it hands the root string to grep exactly as the caller spelled it.
So — when the root is not a directory, the caller has named one file, and no exclusion is passed.
When the root is a directory with a path component ending in `.tetel`, the caller has named inside tetel's own output, and no exclusion is passed.

That one component test is the entire root predicate, and the reason is worth stating because the obvious design has three: the other two artifacts, an evidence ledger and a rendered memo, are files, so a root naming either has already taken the not-a-directory branch and never reaches a content test.
Only for a directory root with no `.tetel` component are the exclusions passed:
`--exclude-dir=*.tetel`, `--exclude=*.evidence.jsonl`, and one `--exclude` per rendered memo, each spelled path-prefixed in the same spelling the root was given in.
Both of the withholding branches are forced rather than chosen, and the next section is why.
NONE
The census predicate does not need to know, and should not be taught to.

`ExtentEntry::censuses` reads five things — the record's kind, its pattern, that its world root is a real git root, and that the search key equals that root — and reads neither the label nor the output.

parts.text: One asymmetry the design cannot close, and should not hide.
Every figure in the replay counts gradings not performed, and a grading is not performed only if some pass declines to perform it.
Nothing here makes that happen.

A brief emits an id, a proposition, an optional pin and a withheld scope per claim, with no instruction prose in either renderer, and the invariant that keeps every claim in the list is the same one this design refused to touch.

This memo designs one change with two halves.

`look` decides for itself how much of an observation it returns to the author, and it says what it withheld in two places: in the observation's label, where a later reader of the memo finds it, and in the returned text itself, where the author finds it before writing anything about what they saw.
The worktree everything below was read against is pinned:

Which of those states each individual fact was captured in is not asserted here: tetel records it with the fact and `check` reports it.

`look_grep` already does the two jobs separately.

It runs grep once, then builds `printed` — the string handed back to the author, which today is grep's stdout verbatim followed by a parenthesised exclusion note — and, independently, the pending entries: one `Search` record carrying the root, the pattern and a matched-file count, and one `GrepMatch` record per matched file carrying that file's matched lines.

The two are derived from the same stdout but neither reads the other, and that separation is what the bound rests on: out of a bounded call, every entry's captured output, its key and its world-tree markers come back byte-identical to what they are today, so two observations of one root still overlap and a later reader still re-reads the same bytes.
What does not stay identical is the extent, the pin and the fact that ships.

`facts::mint` copies each entry's label straight into the extent and hashes label, world markers and output into the pin, and this design writes a shortfall segment into the label — so wherever the bound bites, all three differ from what they would otherwise have been.
That is the point and not a cost.

It is the same property the exclusion note was given when TET-46 chose to list the skipped memo paths rather than count them, so that two searches withholding different things could not fingerprint alike; a bounded search and a whole one should not fingerprint alike either.

What makes f3 cheap, and what keeps it inside the ticket's scope, is narrower than "nothing changes": no new record, no second pass over the buffer, nothing read back out of the entries, no signature touched.
One number is computed while `printed` is being assembled, and the label is built from that number.
The direction matters to whoever implements this — bound first, label from the bound.
An implementer who bounds `printed` and leaves the label alone has rebuilt the silent cut this memo exists to remove.

The donor states that a shortfall is not an error, and the same must hold here: hitting the bound returns a successful outcome with a bounded body, not a refusal.

`check`'s standing non-coverage list gains a line.

That list already distinguishes a withholding tetel chose — its own output, skipped during traversal — from things it merely suffers, like the symlinked directories and binary files the platform's grep never visits; the comment beside them insists a deliberate exclusion earns its own line rather than being folded into a sentence about platform accidents.
A bound tetel applies to its own return is deliberate, so it gets its own line.
That line has two halves, and only the first of them names a verb.

The first half says what f3 bounds, and it cannot be written about a census: the plain path read is inside the bound too and it is a different act — no root, no pattern, no exclusion set, and no filtering of any kind — so a line phrased around what a search returns would leave every bounded file read with no standing statement anywhere.
It says instead that what `look` returned to its author is bounded.
It also has to say what is not:
`run` hands back the whole of a command's captured output unmeasured, on the CLI and over MCP alike, and this design does not change that.
The `run` tool's own description already contemplates a command whose output is enormous and answers it by warning the author rather than by bounding anything.
Naming that exclusion is what keeps the entry honest, because a standing line that named only `look` as bounded would invite a reader to take everything it did not name for whole.

The second half is not verb-scoped, and must not be, because it is true of every observation tetel records however it was taken: a fact's extent records the whole of what was observed, and nothing establishes that the author was shown all of it.
That holds of a command's capture exactly as it holds of a search's or a file read's.
`scope.rs` already registers it as permanently out of reach, so the entry is not an admission of a new weakness but the naming of an old one that had been invisible.

The division of labour between the two is also TET-46's, and it answers the "of what unit" question from the other end.
Every string in the non-coverage list is static and none is per-search, which is why the exclusion set a particular search was given is written into that search's own label instead.

The bound follows the same split, across both bounded paths: the list carries the general statement that what `look` returns to its author is bounded, and each observation's own label carries the numbers for that observation — the search record's label for a search, the path record's for a file read.
Neither place needs the other's job, and neither can do it.

`search: <root> (grep: check) — 70 files matched — showed N of 883 matching lines (32768-byte bound) — <exclusion note>`.
The numerals are there to show the shape; every one of them is computed at run time and will drift as the repository does, and nothing in the design turns on them.
On this HEAD that census is 883 matching lines across 70 files — 70 being the distinct filenames among those matching lines, which is what the file count is computed from.
An earlier draft said 71, from counting distinct filenames over the whole return, in which the trailing exclusion note contributes a spurious extra one.
The unit is matching lines because that is what grep emits and what `look_grep` itself splits on; converting to bytes in the label would report the budget rather than the census.

The file count in front of it needs no change, since it is computed from the full stdout and stays true however little was shown — which is worth noticing, because it means even a heavily bounded return still tells the author truthfully how many files matched.

parts.text: Almost nothing new, and the honest form of that answer matters more than a paging flag would.

The obvious remedies are closed for the case that motivated the ticket: a census is one search of the whole worktree for the symbol itself, so narrowing the root or trimming the pattern does not yield a smaller census, it yields something that is not a census, and `look --grep` has no other parameter to turn.

What an author can do is search a subdirectory as an additional observation standing beside the census rather than replacing it, and — outside the return path entirely — reach the per-file match records, which hold every matched line and ship whole into the snapshot.

So the design's claim is narrow and should be read narrowly: it does not give the author back what was withheld; it stops the withholding from being secret, on the surface they read at the time and in the memo afterwards.
The bounded plain `look <path>` is the easier case:

`--lines A:B` is already a first-class parameter of the same verb, so an author who wants a further whole line of the file asks for it, and each such read keys on the resolved path and therefore overlaps the first.
One residue survives even that, and it is larger than the tail past the cut, so the memo would rather name it exactly than paper it over.

A line longer than the budget is never returned whole by any call, and most ranges containing it return none of it: a range only reaches that line's floored prefix if the line is the *first* one it selects.
Ask for lines 12 to 20 of the longest of the four ledgers and the return is lines 12, 13 and 14 and not one byte of line 15.
So exactly one range start — the line's own position — yields the prefix, every other start yields nothing of the line, and no argument to `look` reaches the remainder past the cut.
Nor does the label point at the position: it reports how many of the selected lines were shown, and on a floored return the byte counts of the line it cut, but never which line overran.

An author who does not already know the position finds it by narrowing the range, and while every such attempt is an ordinary `--lines` read that keys on the same resolved path and stands as its own observation, it is bisection, and the design should say so rather than imply the position is handed over.
Those bytes are recoverable in full only where the grep case's are — in the fact's captured output, which for a file read is the complete selected text and ships in the snapshot beside the memo.

parts.text: One objection deserves answering here rather than later, because it is the one the label invites: this crate does not store derived values, it stores events.

That rule is stated as a reason to recompute what a re-run can obtain from the shipped ledger, and for a search rooted at a directory the shown-count is not obtainable that way — the `Search` entry carries no output, and the per-file entries record what was captured rather than how much of it was handed back, keyed by filename into a map that does not preserve the order the bound consumed.
That argument reaches the recursive search and stops there, and the memo should not let it stand for the verb as a whole.

A grep whose root is a single file is a different instrument reached by the same words: no recursion flag is passed and no exclusions are applied, and the per-file map ends up with one key whose matched lines sit in the order grep printed them, shipped whole as that entry's output under a label naming the file.
The return reconstructs from it, and the count replays out of the reconstruction.
For the path label the count is recoverable too, for a different reason again: that entry's output is the whole of the selected text and `facts.jsonl` ships in the snapshot.
So wherever the number can be recomputed — every file read, and every single-file search — two other things carry it.

The label records what one run showed under the budget that run applied, and the budget is a judgement open to revision, so a later replay answers what today's build would show rather than what this author was shown.

And the audience differs: the doctrine's case is `check` recomputing a report from a ledger it holds, whereas a label is read by someone holding the memo, whose Facts table renders labels and no captured output at all — there is nothing in front of them to recompute from.
That an observation record may carry a measurement beside its bytes is not novel either; the extent already stores the captured output's length.
NONE
The author is the other audience, and the label does not reach them in time.

`look` hands back `printed` and nothing else, on the CLI and over MCP alike; the label first becomes visible one act later, in the `fact` result, by which point the note asserting over that observation has already been supplied as a parameter of the same call.

An author who read a bounded return and then wrote "this is every call site" would have committed the assertion before tetel told them anything had been cut — the design's own defect, reappearing on the surface it exists to fix.
So the shortfall is written into `printed` as well: one `push_str` at the end of a bounded return, carrying the same numbers the label carries.
The crate already has a spelling for this half.

`refuse_incomplete` shortens an undischarged premise to its first line for a refusal message and marks it with a trailing ` …`, applied when and only when something was actually removed. f3 keeps both of those properties — cut on a line boundary, mark only when the bound bit — and adds the one thing that spelling does not carry: how much was withheld.
`refuse_incomplete`'s ellipsis records that text was cut; nothing in its message counts what it dropped, and this design's segment does.
NONE
Where an asymmetry does survive is inside `look_path`, and it is about what a shortfall means rather than about whether the bound applies.

Under `--lines A:B` the author named a range, and the label already records that range as delivered — clamped to the file's length, or an explicit "nothing in range" — so the shortfall it reports is one the author asked for.
A bound biting on top of that is a second shortfall, chosen by tetel rather than by them, and it is recorded beside the first rather than in place of it.

Under a plain `look <path>` there is no author-named range at all: the bound is the only shortfall there is, and naming it is the only thing standing between the author and a cut they would never learn about.

The spelling is the grep case's, on both surfaces: the label reads `<path> — showed N of M lines (32768-byte bound)`, or `<path> lines {a}-{end} — showed N of M lines (32768-byte bound)` where a range was asked for, with M the line count of what was selected before the bound; the returned text ends with the same segment.

The release rule is the grep case's too, floor included — whole lines while a whole line fits, and where none does the first line cut at a character boundary at or below the budget, which the label spells `<path> — showed 0 of M lines; first line cut mid-line at B of L bytes (32768-byte bound)`.
A read that fits gains no segment in either place, and neither case is an error.

The order of the edit has to be stated for this function specifically, because the instruction given earlier — bound first, build the label from the bound — was given about `look_grep`, and `look_grep` is the function whose existing statement order already runs that way.
`look_path` runs the other way.

Its selection and its label are produced together by one `match` on the requested range, and all three arms of that `match` finish the label before the string the bound applies to has been created at all; the label is then handed to the pending entry untouched.

An implementer who bounds the returned string where the selection is pushed into it, and leaves that `match` alone, has written a cut return with a label that says nothing about the cut — the exact defect this memo exists to remove, on the path it was added to last.
So the `match` yields the base label only, and the shortfall segment is appended to it after the release rule has run over the selected text.
NONE
On its own that rule has a hole, and not a hypothetical one — but it is a hole about the first line of a selection, not about a file.
If the first line the rule considers is by itself over budget, no whole line fits, and the return is a header with nothing under it and a label truthfully reporting that nothing was shown.
A file that merely holds a long line somewhere does not produce that state: the accumulation stops before the long line and hands back whatever whole lines preceded it.

Four tracked files in this repository do hold such a line — all of them tetel's own snapshot ledgers, the longest carrying a single line of 905745 bytes — and nothing keeps them out of reach, since a plain `look` refuses only a missing path and a directory and filters nothing at all.

In none of the four, though, is that line the first: the over-budget lines sit at positions 11 and 15 of 20, 15 of 21, 2 of 11 and 2 of 10, so a read that begins at line 1 hands back 5, 2, 1 and 1 whole lines rather than nothing at all.
What reaches the empty state is a selection that begins on such a line, and `--lines` supplies it directly — `--lines 15:20` on the longest of the four, `--lines 2:11` on another.

There the whole-lines-only rule is strictly worse than the silent truncation it exists to replace: a cap that cuts a long line short still hands the author a prefix of it, and this rule hands them none of it.
So the rule takes a floor.

Where no whole line fits, the return carries the first line cut at the largest character boundary at or below the budget, and both surfaces say it was cut mid-line rather than reporting a line count alone.

That gives up something real, and the memo should name it rather than let it pass: a floored return can hand the author a fragment that is not a whole match record, which is the thing the line-boundary rule was chosen to prevent.

What survives the cut is the prefix — a cut grep line still begins `<file>:<lineno>:`, so the fragment still says which match it came from — and the whole line is still in the per-file record that ships.
Against an empty body that is the better trade, and a bounded return is now never empty when what it bounded was not.

In content the design deliberately returns far less than an unbounded caller would, since the budget's one constraint is to sit below a cap tetel cannot observe; in string length it can run a little past its own budget, because the shortfall segment is text a whole return would not have carried and, like the exclusion note, sits outside the measure.
What the floor restores is the promise the design actually makes, which was never to return more but to leave nothing withheld without saying so.

The cut itself has to be spelled out rather than borrowed: nothing in `src` cuts a string at a byte budget today, and these long lines carry multi-byte characters, so the offset is snapped down to a character boundary instead of being taken raw.
NONE
One boundary question has to be settled before the label can be specified, because the label reports a number and the number needs a referent: what exactly is being measured.
`printed` is not simply grep's output.

The parenthesised exclusion note is pushed onto the end of it as a separate segment, on the matching and the no-match branch alike, so a budget applied to the assembled string would eat that note first — it is last.
That would be precisely backwards.

TET-46 put the note into the return because silence about an exclusion is ambiguous between nothing having been hidden and nobody having said so, and the return that most needs to name what it withheld is the one already withholding the most.
So the budget applies to the stdout portion alone.
The note sits outside it, and so does the shortfall segment, which means a bounded return runs a little past the budget by the length of what it says about itself.
The number in the label and in the segment measures the content, not the string.
NONE

parts.text: The sketch left the event's home open between `prose.jsonl` and a sibling log.
The evidence closes it, and not on grounds of taste.
`ProseEvent` is an internally-tagged enum over two variants, and the workspace's line reader turns any single unparseable line into an error over the entire log.
A third variant is therefore not a compatible addition:
I wrote a scratch workspace whose prose log held one ordinary `Create` followed by one `Ack`, and the build at this pin refused the whole file — including the `Create` it understood perfectly well.
Every older build encountering such a snapshot would lose its ability to read prose at all, which is a far worse outcome than the residue line this design exists to clear.
The field-level `#[serde(default)]` precedent already in both variants does not extend to a new variant.
NONE
So the event lives in its own append-only log, `acks.jsonl`, and the snapshot manifest gains a tenth entry.
Three properties, between them, make the failure direction one-way, and the third is the one I had to be shown twice.

The manifest is the first: it is an explicit enumeration precisely so that shipping a new workspace file is a decision rather than an accident, so a build predating the entry never opens the file and prints exactly the listing TET-30 shipped.

The second is that the ack log only grows, which holds cheaply here because the file does not exist yet: nothing in the tool today can remove or truncate a file it has never heard of, its only writer will be an appending verb, and no withdrawal verb ships.
That was where an earlier draft of this section stopped, and stopping there was wrong.
Monotonicity is a property of one workspace's log; the mechanism runs over a snapshot.
Nothing binds a memo to the workspace that rendered it — the flag is free on every invocation — and the writer skips a file the current workspace lacks rather than removing it.

So render a memo once from a workspace holding an acknowledgement, then again from a workspace that never held one — a rebuilt state directory, a second machine — and the old ack log survives beside the new prose and claims.
That is a superset, not a prefix, and it suppresses a block the true state would list, silently.
The third property closes it: the ack records the identity of the workspace that minted it, and suppression requires that identity to match the one the snapshot ships.
A log from elsewhere is then void rather than honoured, and the failure returns to over-reporting.
NONE
Now the problem that buys all of that.
TET-30 names two acts that clear a listing, and for the case this design is about — an edit that corrects the prose and touches no claim's proposition — neither describes what the author did.
Restoring the text puts the typo back.
The other act splits.

Revising a cited claim so its new wording can be graded means changing a claim that is correct, and it is worse than merely expensive: out-of-proof is a machine-check disjunct and this residue is not, so that route turns a green run red and keeps it red until another grounding pass lands, in order to silence a line that by construction never failed anything.

Adding a citation to a freshly minted claim is cheaper — an ungrounded claim is human-owed, so nothing reddens — but it still means inventing a claim the paragraph never needed and buying a pass to grade it.
An author who reads their paragraph against its claims, finds it faithful, and has nothing to change is left with no honest act at all.
That is the defect: not the listing on first appearance, which is informative, but its permanence after the human act it asks for has been performed.
NONE
The brief called deletion and annotation both doctrine-compatible, and they are not equally good.

Deletion loses a distinction the crate elsewhere insists on keeping: a report from which an acknowledged block has vanished cannot be told from a report on a memo where no post-proof revision ever happened, and this is a tool whose no-rows path exists precisely to say that two states which happen to both be quiet are not the same state.

The cost of printing is also already paid — the entry format carries an author's own reason verbatim today, under `revised because:`, with the source comment insisting it is never paraphrased and calling it the most actionable line the entry has.
NONE
So an acknowledged block moves rather than disappears.

It leaves the group under the "prose revised after the claims it cites settled" preamble — which is what makes the acknowledgement feel like a discharge and not a footnote — and reappears under a single collapsed bullet listing, per block, its id, its line in the document, when it was acknowledged, and the author's own words for why.

Because the reason and the timestamp are recorded but not keyed, more than one ack can match a block at once, and the entry prints the earliest of them: that mirrors the trigger's own use of the earliest event bearing the current wording, and it shows a reader the moment the discharge was first made rather than the latest restatement of it.
The collapse itself is the crate's habit: the residue's preamble is one document-level bullet, adopted on the stated ground that a constant repeated per row buries what is specific to this document.
Leaving the entry in place with an annotation stapled to it would keep the demand standing after it had been met, which is exactly the condition that teaches readers to skim the partition.
NONE

The event records the block, the block's current text and citation list, a digest of each cited claim's proposition as it stands at that moment, the identity of the workspace minting it, and the author's verbatim reason; it carries a timestamp because every workspace event does.

A listing is suppressed exactly when some ack for that block matches all of that, byte for byte, against values the check recomputes — the digests included, and the identity against the one the snapshot itself ships.
One detail here is easy to get wrong and I got it wrong first: the digests are taken over the claim as `claims.jsonl` holds it, not over the ledger-derived proposition the in-proof test must use.

Those two strings differ — rendering replaces embedded newlines with spaces and importing trims the cell — so keying the ack on the trigger's digest would make any claim with an embedded newline or edge whitespace permanently unackable, silently.
Both sides of the ack's comparison read the same source, and the snapshot already ships it.
No timestamp is compared anywhere in the predicate.
NONE
The sketch also wanted the ack's timestamp compared against the recomputed anchor.
Working through when that comparison could ever decide anything showed it cannot.

The rule is only ever consulted for a block the trigger has already listed, and listing is precisely the statement that the block timestamp exceeds the anchor; the ack is appended afterwards, to an append-only log, by the same workspace and the same clock function that stamped the prose event.
Barring a clock set backwards mid-session, the ack timestamp is above the block timestamp which is above the anchor, so the clause is true every time it is asked.

Removing it is not a simplification for its own sake — it leaves the suppression predicate with no timestamp comparison anywhere in it, and so the acknowledgement, alone among the moving parts here, does not inherit the two-clock bound that the trigger's own preamble has to print.
NONE
Three properties are worth stating as invariants with tests, and each has a specific mutation that should turn its test red.

Any later edit to the block's text or citations voids the ack, since both are in the key — weaken the comparison to text alone and a citation-only revision, which TET-30 deliberately made list rather than clear, would slip through an old acknowledgement.

Any change to a cited claim's proposition voids the ack, since the key carries that claim's digest — drop the digests and an acknowledgement survives a rewrite of the very claim the paragraph was read against.

And for a memo whose snapshot carries no acknowledgement log, the residue reports exactly what it reports today, because the line reader treats a missing file as an empty log; make that an error instead and every memo rendered before this design would stop checking.

That third invariant is deliberately stated over the residue's findings rather than the report's bytes, because this same design adds lines to the non-coverage list, which prints unconditionally and so changes the bytes of every report the tool will ever write.
It is also about the snapshot and not the workspace, which is worth saying explicitly rather than leaving to be inferred: the check never sees a workspace.
NONE
Underneath those is the property that makes the rest cheap to reason about: the acknowledgement is a filter applied to the trigger's output, never an input to it.
The set of blocks a reader is asked to act on can only shrink, so the design cannot invent a demand.
A stale ack and an unmatched ack both simply fail to suppress, which is indistinguishable from no ack at all.
A corrupt one is the case I first waved through and should not have.

The line reader turns any bad line into an error over the entire log, and the one place this crate swallows that silently — the prose log at check time — defends the silence with a premise that does not transfer: that a corrupt prose log has already reddened provenance before the check gets there.
Keeping acks out of `render` is precisely what makes that false for this file.

So an unreadable acknowledgement log has to redden, joining the existing rule that drift and an unreadable snapshot are machine failures because both are objective contradictions decidable without a human.
That is the single point where this design touches the machine partition, and it touches it for corruption of the record rather than for anything an acknowledgement means.
It is also worth being clear what the digests do not buy: keying on them does not close TET-30's conceded blind spot for prose that ships alongside a claim revision.
It only stops an acknowledgement outliving the state it attested to.
NONE
There is exactly one verb — `prose --ack <id> --why <text>`, on both front ends — and, as the section on withdrawal explains, deliberately no second one.

It is added to the shared request shape the CLI and the MCP server already funnel through, and here I have to correct something an earlier draft of this memo asserted: that shape is necessary for the two front ends to agree, and it is not sufficient.
This verb is the case that proves it, twice over, both times about text.

An acknowledgement carries none, but the MCP parameter struct declares text as a plain required string while the CLI declares it optional — so an ack over MCP is refused by deserialisation before any of the tool's own refusals are reached, and the same ack over the CLI sails through.
Relaxing that field is part of this design.
But relaxing it is not enough, because an absent `--text` on the CLI does not mean absent: both text-consuming arms resolve it through a helper whose empty case reads standard input.
Left alone, an acknowledgement with no text would sit there blocking on stdin.
So `--text` has to be refused outright in this mode, and the ack arm placed where it can never reach that fallback.
NONE
There is a second thing each front end does that this verb must not inherit.

Mode is selected by an if/else-if chain that builds one request variant and silently drops whatever inputs that variant has no field for, so an ack combined with `--text`, `--revise`, `--heading`, `--level`, `--cites` or `--before` would discard one without a word — the same shape as the defect this crate already had to fix once, when citations were accepted alongside a revision and thrown away.
All six have to be refused, and `--level` is worth dwelling on because I left it out and an attack pass had to put it back.
On the CLI it is its own flag, consumed by the heading arm but selected by `--heading`; over MCP the two are folded into a single field that is selector and value at once.
An enumeration written while looking at the MCP shape cannot see the CLI's seventh flag.

Of the ack's remaining refusals only two already exist: the block must exist, and `--why` must be non-empty, the latter on literally the test that backs the revise verb's insistence that revisions explain themselves.
Three are new, because creation is deliberately ungated — refusing a heading, refusing an uncited block, and refusing a citation that names no claim.
Each earns its place: a listing exists for neither a heading nor an uncited block, and the ack's key is a digest per cited claim, which an unresolvable id cannot supply.
One refusal that might seem obvious is impossible.

The verb cannot decline to acknowledge a block that is not currently listed, because an authoring workspace holds prose, claims, facts, targets and counters and no evidence records whatsoever — grading records live beside the rendered memo — so at mint time there is no anchor to compute.
Nor is it wanted: acknowledging an unlisted block suppresses nothing.
NONE
Because the residue is computed against a snapshot and the snapshot is written by `render --out`, an ack minted after a render is invisible until the next one.
That sequencing is not new and it is not this design's to fix: everything the check sees about a workspace it sees through the snapshot.

What is this design's to decide is whether the acknowledgement changes the memo's bytes, and it must not — the determinism of `render` in the workspace alone is what makes a drift finding mean anything.

Keeping acks out of the rendered output turns the extra render from an annoyance into a useful signal: it rewrites the snapshot in place and leaves the document byte-identical, so the discharge lands in version control as a change to the record with no change to the argument.
That is a true description of what an acknowledgement is.
NONE
Supersession asks nothing of the design.
Matching is existential over keys, so a later ack with a different key simply does not match, and a duplicate ack for the same key cannot change whether a block is suppressed.
Withdrawal is the harder question, and I have been wrong about it in both directions.
I first designed an `Unack` event, on the reasoning that an author who acknowledged too quickly and cannot yet rewrite the paragraph would otherwise have nothing to say.
Then I removed it, on the reasoning that a negative event is uniquely droppable — and that reasoning survives, though it turned out to matter for a different reason than I gave.

Declining the verb is what keeps the ack log monotone, and monotonicity is what makes a stale snapshot copy a prefix rather than an arbitrary earlier state, which is the whole one-directional guarantee of the section above.

An `Unack` would have broken it: a render by a build predating the log leaves it where the last knowing render put it, so a withdrawal appended afterwards vanishes while the acknowledgement it cancelled survives — the one path by which a negative event is lost and a positive one is not.
And the decision stands on a second leg that was always the stronger.

The case an `Unack` protects is not symmetric with the defect this design exists for: an author who now believes the paragraph is faulty can repair the paragraph, which voids the acknowledgement by changing its key.
That is an honest act, and it is the one they should be taking.
TET-30's defect was precisely that a correct paragraph left its author no act at all.
NONE

a duplicate ack for the same key cannot change whether a block is suppressed

parts.text: Eleven symbols change, and the whole-worktree census of each is what lets that be said rather than hoped.

On the check side the obvious four: the rule function takes the acks as a further input and returns two partitions instead of one list, bounded by there being exactly one production call site among its thirty-three; the findings field gains a sibling; the snapshot manifest goes from nine entries to ten; the non-coverage list gains entries.
The snapshot writer, which an earlier draft would have changed, is untouched.

Then three more that an attack pass had to find, because they are the price of reddening a corrupt ack log: a new findings field reddens nothing by itself, so the machine-check disjunction gains a term, the failure count — a hand-written sum linked to that disjunction by nothing but discipline — gains another, and the literal naming the machine-checked categories gains a twelfth.

The authoring side added four more across two passes: two enums consumed by exhaustive matches, a parameter type where the front ends had already drifted on whether text is required, and a flag declaration living on the variant rather than the dispatch arm.

And then, on the last pass, three enumerations of those same categories that no census reaches at all — the README, the MCP tool description that agents read as the schema, and the printed human-owed headline that TET-30 itself had to hand-edit to announce this very residue, and that the acknowledged bullet obliges someone to edit again.
The honest summary is not the count.
It is that this memo has now been short by one on three separate enumerations, found by three separate passes, and that an implementer should re-derive every list here rather than trust it.
NONE

llm_findings.clause: the front ends had already drifted on whether text is required

parts.text: Stated upfront, before the argument that gets there: the discharge is a new workspace event in its own append-only log, keyed on the block's current text, its citation list, a digest of each cited claim, and the identity of the workspace that minted it — suppressing the listing exactly while all of that still matches what the check recomputes.
A tenth file therefore ships in the snapshot and a new event schema exists, falsifying deliberately the sentence TET-30's memo ends its implementation-surface claim with.
The payment is bounded, but by three properties rather than the two an earlier draft claimed, and only two of them come free: a predating build never opens the new file, and the ack log only grows.

The third had to be added, because a memo is not bound to the workspace that rendered it, and without the identity component a snapshot can carry acknowledgements no workspace on the machine ever made.
The cost also has two shapes, not one.
Ordinarily an older build over-reports a line a newer one suppresses.
But because a corrupt ack log reddens, one malformed line makes a new build exit 1 where an old build runs clean — a disagreement about the machine partition rather than about a listing.

`check` names the binary behind every report it writes, so either divergence is attributable; what that does not cover is a reader holding a single old report, with nothing in it to suggest an acknowledgement exists.
For them the answer is the log itself, plain JSON lines beside the memo, readable with no tetel at all.
NONE

Three lines are owed in the printed non-coverage list, on the list's own standard that a deliberate exclusion earns its own line because a refusal that fired reads too easily as coverage it never claimed.

One: an acknowledgement records that a human said they re-read the paragraph against its claims, and nothing verifies that they did or judges whether the paragraph is faithful — after an ack, the tool's silence is the author's assertion and not the tool's finding.
Two: an acknowledgement minted after the last render is not in the snapshot the check reads, and suppresses nothing until the memo is rendered again.
Three, for the reason the closing section gives: a snapshot's acknowledgement log is never re-rendered, so a hand-edited one is invisible to the drift check.
NONE
The advisory recommendation that per-citation attribution be folded into the ack rather than into the trigger is accepted, and it is worth being blunt that the fold does not go far.

The residue's own non-coverage list already concedes that whether a paragraph was examined against an earlier-settled co-citation is answered by no listing, and the acknowledgement does not answer it: the ack is per block, its key records only that every cited claim's digest was what it was, and the sole place a per-citation judgement can live is inside the author's verbatim reason, which nothing should parse.

So the acknowledged bullet prints the block's cited claim ids beside that reason, letting a reader pair the author's words to the citations themselves, and the non-coverage entry stays exactly where it is.
NONE
When the full obligation ledger lands, these events are the discharge records it would consume for this residue class, and the log moves into it unrewritten.

That works because nothing in an ack is specific to the check it discharges: it holds a block id, a text, a citation list, a digest per cited claim, a reason and a timestamp, and none of the quantities the rule derives — not the anchor, not any claim's first proof, not the block timestamp, not even whether the block was listed.
The general ledger needs the events as they stand plus a rule that reads them, which is a re-homing and not a rework.
NONE

One line on the separate question of warning an author when they revise prose whose claims have settled: this design does not settle it and does not depend on it, but it does change its economics, since such a warning today could name no act and afterwards could name this one.
Whether it is worth building stays a measurement question, unanswered here.
NONE

llm_findings.clause: such a warning today could name no act

parts.text: One thing remains to be said, and it belongs with the decision to keep acknowledgements out of the rendered bytes.
Drift is decided by re-rendering the snapshot, and `render` reads exactly five of the nine files a snapshot ships — prose, claims, targets, transplants and facts.

The other four are shipped and never re-rendered, so tampering with them is not drift, and one of those four is the identity file, which already decides whether the report calls a claim self-grounded or independently grounded.
An acknowledgement log joins that group rather than founding it.

A hand-edited snapshot ack log is therefore undetectable by drift, and the honest response is a non-coverage line rather than a bespoke mechanism: guarding acks alone would leave the four existing members unguarded while implying they were not.
That is the last of this design's costs, and like the others it is meant to be read rather than absorbed.
NONE
